name: Kurseong, Mirik & the tea valleys
tagline: Tea slopes, a lake town and Netaji's hill
meta_description: Plan Kurseong, Mirik, Makaibari, Sittong and Latpanchar on a budget: the real local history, shared jeep fares, homestay prices and the best months.
summary: Kurseong and Mirik are the two hill towns of the middle Darjeeling hills, an hour or two above Siliguri. Between them lie tea gardens such as Makaibari and Gopaldhara, the orange village of Sittong and the hornbill forests of Latpanchar. Homestays run ₹1,200–2,000 per person with meals; shared jeeps cost ₹150–250.

story.title: The middle hills between the plains and Darjeeling
paras: Kurseong was hill country that changed hands more than once before the British arrived. Nepal's Gorkha armies took the area around 1780; the Treaty of Titalia in 1817 handed it back to Sikkim; and from 1835, when the East India Company took the Darjeeling tract as a sanatorium, the slopes below Darjeeling were opened up for roads, tea and schools. Kurseong became a municipality in 1879, the same decade the Darjeeling Himalayan Railway was being pushed up the hill, and a subdivision in 1890.

Tea shaped everything after that. Makaibari, just below Kurseong, commissioned its factory in 1859, and the Banerjee family ran the estate for four generations. West of the Balason river, Nepali sardars and later planters cleared the Mirik valley: Soureni's tea was formally established in 1902, and Gopaldhara traces its first planting to 1881. The workers who came from eastern Nepal brought Nepali, which is still the language of these hills, alongside the older Lepcha place names.

The twentieth century left its own marks. Subhas Chandra Bose was held under house arrest in his brother's house at Giddapahar in 1936. A Jesuit seminary taught on St Mary's Hill from 1889 to 1971. In the 1970s a marsh at Mirik was turned into Sumendu Lake, opened in 1979, and Tibetan Buddhist teacher Bokar Rinpoche founded his monastery above it in 1984. Today the land lives on tea, oranges, schools and small-scale tourism.

intro: This land covers the hills between Siliguri and Darjeeling: Kurseong town and its ridge of old schools at Dow Hill, the tea gardens of Makaibari and Ambootia below it, the Riyang valley villages of Sittong and Latpanchar to the east, and Mirik with its tea valleys of Soureni, Tingling and Gopaldhara to the west. Most of it sits between 1,200 and 2,200 m, warmer than Darjeeling and greener, with fewer crowds.

It is the easiest part of the Darjeeling hills to do cheaply. Kurseong is about 1.5–2 hours from Siliguri by shared jeep, Mirik about 2–2.5 hours, and both have a good spread of small hotels and homestays. Village homestays in Sittong, Latpanchar, Chimney and the Makaibari estate charge ₹1,200–2,000 per person including dinner and breakfast, and that price usually includes local food you would not find in a hotel.

Come for the stories as much as the views. Kurseong's name is usually traced to a Lepcha word for a white orchid. Netaji's letters went out from a house on Giddapahar. Makaibari's name means cornfield. Mirik's name, in Lepcha, means a place burnt by fire. We tell those stories place by place, and then the jeep fares, the homestay rates and the months to go.
facts: Kurseong ≈ 35–50 km · 1.5–2 h; Mirik ≈ 52 km · 2–2.5 h
None for Indian or foreign visitors

highlights.title: Netaji's house at Giddapahar
highlights.text: Sarat Chandra Bose bought this house above Kurseong in 1922, and his brother Subhas was held here under house arrest by the British in 1936. It is now a small museum of letters, photographs and furniture, and the road up gives wide views of the plains.

highlights.title: A night inside Makaibari
highlights.text: The estate's village homestay programme puts you in a tea worker's family house with dinner and breakfast, at a fraction of a planter's bungalow price. Walk the plucking paths at 7 am and see the factory that first ran in 1859.

highlights.title: Sittong in orange season
highlights.text: From November to January the Riyang valley village of Sittong is heavy with Darjeeling mandarins. Homestays sell them by the basket, the cinchona directorate has organised an orange festival in December, and the walk down to the river is a gentle half-day.

highlights.title: Hornbills at Latpanchar
highlights.text: Latpanchar is the highest part of Mahananda Wildlife Sanctuary, and its old trees draw rufous-necked and great hornbills. Bird with a local guide at dawn, then climb Ahaldara for the Teesta valley and, on a clear morning, Kanchenjunga.

highlights.title: Mirik's lake and monastery
highlights.text: Sumendu Lake has a 3.5 km path round it, rowing boats and a footbridge, and above it sits Bokar Monastery, founded by Bokar Rinpoche in 1984. Mornings are quiet; afternoons fill with day-trippers from Siliguri.

highlights.title: Tingling and the tea bowls
highlights.text: On the road from Dudhia to Mirik, Tingling viewpoint looks across rolling tea estates to the Balason valley on one side and Nepal's Mechi valley on the other. Gopaldhara, higher up, grows tea at up to about 2,100 m.

getting_there: Fly to Bagdogra or take a train to New Jalpaiguri (NJP), then go via Siliguri. Shared jeeps for Kurseong leave from the Hill Cart Road stands near Siliguri Junction and Tenzing Norgay bus terminus, ₹150–200 a seat, 1.5–2 hours by Rohini road or 2–2.5 hours by the old Hill Cart Road. Shared jeeps for Mirik go via Matigara and Dudhia, ₹150–200 a seat, about 2–2.5 hours. A reserved car from NJP or Bagdogra costs about ₹2,000–2,800 to Kurseong and ₹2,200–3,000 to Mirik. Sittong and Latpanchar have few shared jeeps: most people hire a car (₹3,000–3,800 from Siliguri). The toy train reaches Kurseong on the NJP–Darjeeling line when it runs; schedules change with landslides, so check current status before you travel.
money: This is one of the cheapest corners of the Darjeeling hills. A shoestring day costs ₹1,500–2,000: a shared jeep seat for ₹150–200, a homestay bed with dinner and breakfast for ₹1,200–1,600, momos and tea for ₹100–150, and free walks. A comfortable day runs ₹3,500–5,000 with a private car for sightseeing (₹2,500–3,500 a day) and a hotel room with a view. People overspend in three places: hiring a car for a single passenger when shared jeeps run the same road, booking 'package' sightseeing in Mirik that covers five stops you can walk to, and paying lake-side hotel prices on Durga Puja weekends. Prices are indicative for 2025–26.

months.summary: Cold, clear and quiet. Mornings are the best of the year for distant views, with Kanchenjunga visible from Ahaldara and the higher Kurseong ridges on many days. Oranges are still being picked around Sittong and Mirik. Rooms without heaters are cold, so ask before booking, and pack thermals. Prices are low outside the New Year week, and the town is mostly local life. On 23 January Kurseong marks Netaji's birth anniversary at Giddapahar.
months.tip: Book a homestay with a heater or a bukhari stove and carry a hot-water bottle.

months.summary: Days warm up and the air stays mostly dry, though haze from the plains creeps in late in the month. Tea gardens are pruned and bare, which is not the best time for factory visits, but the walking is good. Losar, the Tibetan New Year, usually falls in February or March and is marked at Bokar Monastery in Mirik. A good month for budget travellers who want quiet roads and low homestay prices.
months.tip: Losar dates follow the Tibetan lunar calendar, so check the date for the year before you plan around it.

months.summary: First flush begins. Plucking restarts in the gardens of Makaibari, Gopaldhara and the Mirik valley, factories start running and the young leaf is picked for the most prized teas of the year. Rhododendron and magnolia flower on the higher ridges around Chimney. Views are good in the mornings and hazier by afternoon. Book ahead for Holi week, when Bengal's holiday crowd arrives.
months.tip: Ask a garden homestay host when plucking starts on their section; it varies by height.

months.summary: Warm, green and busy in the gardens. First flush is in full swing, birdlife at Latpanchar is active and the forests around Dow Hill fill with new leaf. Afternoon thunderstorms start late in the month. School holidays in the plains push up prices in Mirik and Kurseong around mid-April, so book early. A good month for tea and birds, less so for mountain views.
months.tip: Go to Latpanchar at dawn; hornbills are most active before 9 am.

months.summary: The main summer holiday month for families from Kolkata and the plains. Mirik's lake is at its busiest and Kurseong's hotels fill on weekends. The second flush starts toward the end of May. Thunderstorms are more frequent and roads can get slow. Stay in villages rather than towns to find quieter rooms and lower prices.
months.tip: Visit Mirik's lake before 9 am, when the day-trip cars from Siliguri have not yet arrived.

months.summary: The first half is still pleasant; the monsoon usually reaches the hills by mid-June. Second-flush tea is being made, which is the muscatel season Darjeeling is famous for. Expect rain most afternoons and occasional road slowdowns at Pagla Jhora and on the Rohini road. Prices start to drop. Namthing Pokhri fills and the Himalayan salamanders begin to come out to breed.
months.tip: Keep a buffer day before a flight: landslides on the Hill Cart Road can close it for hours.

months.summary: The heaviest rain of the year. Landslides are common on the Kurseong roads, especially around Pagla Jhora and Tindharia, and views are rare. Mahananda sanctuary is closed to visitors in the monsoon. For a writer, a reader or a tea lover with time, a garden homestay at half-season prices can still be good. Otherwise, skip it.
months.tip: If you come, stay put in one place and check road status each morning.

months.summary: Still wet, still green, still prone to landslides. Leeches are out on forest walks. Namthing Pokhri is at its fullest and the salamander season is under way, though you must keep to the edge and not handle the animals. Prices are at their lowest. Most travellers are better off coming in October.
months.tip: Carry salt or leech socks on any forest path.

months.weather: Kurseong 16–21 °C, rain easing late in the month
months.summary: The rain eases through the month and the hills are at their greenest. Autumn-flush tea begins. Late September sometimes brings the first clear morning views. Durga Puja falls in late September or October and brings a big rush from Bengal, so book a room early. Dashain, the main festival of the Nepali-speaking hills, often begins around the same time.
months.tip: If Puja falls in your dates, book transport both ways in advance.

months.summary: One of the best months. The air clears after the rain, Kanchenjunga shows from Ahaldara and the high ridges, and the tea gardens make autumn flush. Dashain and Tihar light up Kurseong's lanes, with tika, swings and oil lamps. It is also the busiest month of the year, with Puja and Diwali holidays, so book stays and jeeps early.
months.tip: Be at Ahaldara by sunrise; by 10 am clouds often climb out of the Teesta valley.

months.summary: Our favourite month. Crowds thin after Diwali, mornings are reliably clear and oranges start to colour in Sittong and around Mirik. It is the best time for walks between Dow Hill and Chimney and for birding at Latpanchar. Nights get cold enough for a jacket, and homestays begin offering winter discounts later in the month.
months.tip: Buy oranges from the orchard owner, not the roadside; they are cheaper and fresher.

months.summary: Orange season peaks. The Directorate of Cinchona has organised an orange festival at Sittong in December. Clear skies give the best mountain views from Ahaldara and the Kurseong ridges. Christmas week brings a short rush to Mirik and Kurseong, where the town churches hold services and carols. Otherwise, prices are low and the days are bright and cold.
months.tip: Pack gloves and a warm hat for sunrise; the wind on Ahaldara is sharp.

faqs.q: Is Kurseong or Mirik better for a short trip?
faqs.a: Kurseong is better if you like history, walks and the toy train: Netaji's house, Dow Hill, Eagle's Crag and Makaibari are all within 10 km. Mirik is better for a relaxed family trip around a lake, with tea viewpoints at Tingling and Soureni on the way. With three nights, do one night in Kurseong and two in Mirik, or the other way round.

faqs.q: How do I get from Siliguri to Kurseong cheaply?
faqs.a: Take a shared jeep from the Hill Cart Road stands near Siliguri Junction or the Tenzing Norgay bus terminus. Seats cost about ₹150–200 and the ride takes 1.5–2 hours on the Rohini road or 2–2.5 hours on the old Hill Cart Road. Jeeps leave when full, roughly every 30–45 minutes in the morning, fewer after 3 pm.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for Kurseong, Mirik or Sittong?
faqs.a: No. Kurseong, Mirik, Sittong, Latpanchar and the tea gardens are in West Bengal and need no permit for Indian or foreign travellers. Mahananda Wildlife Sanctuary charges entry for some areas and closes in the monsoon. If you continue into Sikkim, foreign nationals need a Restricted Area Permit; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Kurseong and Mirik?
faqs.a: October to December is best for clear views, with November the quietest of the three. March to May is best for tea, with first flush in March and April and birds active at Latpanchar. Avoid July and August, when heavy rain brings landslides on the Hill Cart Road and the Rohini road and views are rare.

faqs.q: How much does a budget trip to Kurseong and Mirik cost?
faqs.a: A careful backpacker can do it on ₹1,500–2,000 a day: shared jeeps at ₹150–200 a seat, a homestay with dinner and breakfast at ₹1,200–1,600, and free walks. A couple in a mid-range hotel with a car for sightseeing will spend ₹3,500–5,000 per person per day. Our 2025–26 journeys start at about ₹5,500 per person for two nights.

faqs.q: Can I stay inside a Darjeeling tea garden on a budget?
faqs.a: Yes. The Makaibari estate below Kurseong runs a village homestay programme in which tea workers' families host guests, usually around ₹1,500–2,000 per person with meals. Several homestays also sit on garden land around Mirik, Sittong and Ambootia. Ask the host to arrange a factory visit and an early plucking walk.

faqs.q: Does the toy train still stop at Kurseong?
faqs.a: Kurseong is a station on the Darjeeling Himalayan Railway between NJP and Darjeeling, and the line runs right through the town's bazaar. Services on the lower section have been suspended for long periods by landslides, including at Pagla Jhora and Tindharia from 2010 to 2015. Book on IRCTC and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is Mirik worth visiting in the monsoon?
faqs.a: Only if you want rain, mist and low prices. From late June to August Mirik is green and quiet, but views are rare, the lake path is slippery and the Dudhia road can be slowed by small landslides. Late September is a better compromise: the rain is easing, the tea gardens are green and Puja crowds have not yet peaked.

faqs.q: Can I combine Kurseong and Mirik with Darjeeling?
faqs.a: Yes, easily. Kurseong is about 32 km below Darjeeling (1.5 hours by shared jeep, ₹100–150), and Mirik is about 49 km from Darjeeling by the Sukhia Pokhari road (about 2 hours). A loop of Siliguri, Mirik, Darjeeling, Kurseong and back to Siliguri works well in five or six nights.

to_confirm: Kurseong's name: commonly traced to Lepcha 'Kharsang', 'land of the white orchid'; Wikipedia also gives 'small orchid' and a cane-stick derivation. We present it as the usual explanation.
Netaji museum at Giddapahar: Sarat Bose bought the house in 1922, Netaji under house arrest there in 1936 (sources say about seven months), museum since about 2000. Opening days and fee to confirm.
Makaibari: estate cleared in the 1850s (Wikipedia says 1852 by Captain Samler), factory 1859; homestay rates ₹1,500–2,000 pp are indicative only.
Dow Hill Girls' School founding year (1890s?) and whether the Dow Hill forest museum is open to visitors.
Chimney: local accounts date the dak bungalow chimney to about 1839 and give its height as about 23 ft; altitude about 2,200 m is approximate.
Sittong church: described locally as an old bamboo church now rebuilt in brick, about a century old; no exact year found.
Sittong Orange Festival: Wikipedia says the Directorate of Cinchona organises it every December; confirm it is still held each year.
Ahaldara altitude (we say about 1,500 m) and the exact walking distance from the car park.
Gopaldhara: planting from 1881 and the 'Gopal's stream' name origin are the estate's own account; a roadside tea shop is mentioned by travellers but not confirmed.
Himalayan salamander at Namthing Pokhri: described as Tylototriton himalayanus in 2015; many local sources still say T. verrucosus.
Cochrane Place: confirm current tariffs; listed as a mid-to-upper-range heritage hotel.
GTA Swiss Cottages in Mirik: confirm booking channel and current operation.
